chapter_summary:
Even the most robust RHEL systems can encounter performance issues or become unresponsive. As a system administrator, your ability to quickly diagnose and troubleshoot these problems is critical. Performance tuning begins with identifying bottlenecks. The four primary resources to monitor are CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network. A high load on any of these can degrade overall system performance. Understanding which resource is constrained is the first step towards a solution. For instance, a server with high CPU utilization might indicate a runaway process or an application performing intensive computations, while excessive disk I/O could point to a database issue or heavy logging.

Several command-line tools are indispensable for real-time monitoring and initial diagnosis.
*   **`top`**: Provides a dynamic, real-time view of running processes. It shows CPU usage, memory usage, swap usage, and system load averages. You can sort processes by CPU (`P`) or memory (`M`) usage to quickly identify resource hogs. `top` is excellent for a quick overview, but its interface can be a bit dense for beginners.
*   **`htop`**: An enhanced, interactive version of `top` that offers a more user-friendly interface, color-coded output, and easy navigation. It allows you to scroll, kill processes, and view process trees more intuitively. If available, `htop` is often preferred for its ease of use.
*   **`vmstat`**: Reports virtual memory statistics. It provides information about processes, memory, paging, block I/O, traps, and CPU activity. Running `vmstat 1` will show updates every second, allowing you to observe trends. High values in `si` (swap in) or `so` (swap out) columns indicate excessive swapping, suggesting a memory bottleneck.
*   **`iostat`**: Reports CPU utilization and disk I/O statistics. Using `iostat -x 1` provides extended statistics, including `%util` (percentage of time the device is busy), `r/s` (reads per second), `w/s` (writes per second), and `avgqu-sz` (average queue length). High `%util` or `avgqu-sz` values point to a disk I/O bottleneck.
*   **`ss` / `netstat`**: These tools (with `ss` being the modern replacement for `netstat`) display network connections, routing tables, interface statistics, and more. `ss -tunap` shows TCP and UDP connections, including the process ID (PID) and program name associated with each connection. This is invaluable for identifying processes consuming network bandwidth or listening on unexpected ports.

When a system becomes unresponsive, a systematic approach is key. First, try to identify if it's a specific application or the entire system. Check system load averages (`uptime` or `top`), memory usage, and swap activity. If a process is consuming excessive resources, you might need to terminate it using `kill` or `kill -9` (the latter is a forceful termination and should be used as a last resort). A common mistake is to immediately reboot, which often clears valuable diagnostic information. Instead, gather data first. Check recent kernel messages with `dmesg` for hardware errors or critical system events. Review system logs (`journalctl` and `/var/log/messages`, `/var/log/secure`) for any error messages or unusual activity preceding the issue.

For deeper troubleshooting, especially with application-specific problems:
*   **`strace`**: Traces system calls and signals. If an application is crashing or behaving unexpectedly, `strace` can reveal which system calls are failing or what files it's trying to access. For example, `strace -p <PID>` attaches to a running process, or `strace <COMMAND>` runs a command and traces it.
*   **`lsof` (List Open Files)**: Shows all open files and the processes that opened them. This includes regular files, directories, network sockets, and pipes. `lsof -i` shows open network connections, and `lsof /path/to/file` shows which process has a specific file open. This is incredibly useful for debugging "resource busy" errors or identifying processes holding onto deleted files.

Performance tuning often involves a cycle of monitoring, identifying bottlenecks, making changes (e.g., adjusting application configuration, adding resources, optimizing queries), and then re-monitoring. For example, if `iostat` shows high disk I/O, you might investigate the application's logging configuration, database queries, or consider moving to faster storage. If `vmstat` shows heavy swapping, you might need to add more RAM or optimize memory usage of applications. Always document your changes and monitor the impact. Effective troubleshooting and performance tuning are continuous processes that refine your understanding of the system and its applications.

screens.title: Basic Troubleshooting and Performance Tuning
screens.subtitle: Learn to find bottlenecks, use real‑time monitoring tools, and take safe first steps for unresponsive systems

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn a practical, calm approach to diagnosing and tuning RHEL systems. We focus on the four primary bottlenecks — C P U, memory, disk input and output and network — and the toolbox you will use: top and htop for process-level insight, vmstat for virtual memory trends, iostat for disk activity, and ss for network sockets. You will also see when to collect deeper diagnostics with dmesg, strace and lsof. The goal is not to memorize every flag but to develop a repeatable workflow: monitor, identify the constrained resource, gather targeted evidence, make a conservative change, then re‑measure. I will give clear examples you can run in a lab: simulating a C P U hog, observing swap activity, watching disk util spikes, and tracing a misbehaving process. We’ll also stress common mistakes — for example, rebooting immediately or using kill -9 as a first response — and how to avoid losing diagnostic information. By the end, you’ll have a mental checklist for rapid triage and a handful of commands that reliably point you to the root cause. Ready to build a diagnostic habit that protects system data and saves time?

keyIdea.title: Practical triage first
keyIdea.text: Identify which resource is constrained (CPU, memory, disk I/O, network) before making changes; gather evidence with monitoring tools and logs first.

narration.text: By the end of these lessons you will be routinely able to identify which of the four primary resources — C P U, memory, disk input and output, or network — is causing system slowdown. You will learn to use standard RHEL utilities such as top, htop, vmstat, iostat, and ss to gather live metrics and spot anomalies. You will practice a structured triage process that preserves diagnostic data and avoids premature reboots. Each objective pairs a skill with why it matters: being able to spot swap activity with vmstat prevents misdiagnosis; knowing how to read iostat avoids chasing the wrong problem when disks are saturated; using ss lets you correlate active sockets with processes. You will also learn when to escalate to deeper tools like dmesg, strace, and lsof for kernel messages, syscall tracing, and open file inspection. These competencies let you act quickly, safely, and with evidence, which reduces downtime and preserves logs for root cause analysis.

keyIdea.title: Evidence-driven troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Skillful admins collect the right metrics first, then act; the objective is reproducible diagnosis, not guesswork.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Tool Skills

Tools & Diagnostics

Practice interpreting each tool’s primary metric so you can quickly map symptoms to root cause.

Mnemonic Grid
top / htop — Processes & CPU
vmstat — si / so (swap signs)
iostat — %util / avgqu-sz
ss — sockets to PID mapping
Verification Tasks
  1. Run vmstat 1 and interpret si/so trend.
  2. Capture iostat -x 1 during heavy writes and note %util.
  3. Use ss -tunap to find processes with many connections.

screens.title: Performance Bottlenecks: CPU, Memory, Disk I/O, Network
screens.subtitle: Define the four resource classes and how they limit overall system performance

narration.text: A performance bottleneck is any resource whose limited capacity constrains the whole system. In RHEL we focus on four classes: C P U, memory, disk input and output, and network. C P U bottlenecks occur when processor time is saturated and processes wait on the C P U, often seen as high user or system C P U percentages and high run queue length. Memory bottlenecks manifest as frequent swapping; vmstat’s si and so columns show swap in and swap out, and high values there mean the kernel is moving pages between R A M and disk, which is much slower than R A M. Disk input and output bottlenecks appear as high device utilization and long queues; iostat reports %util and avgqu-sz — when %util approaches 100% or queue lengths grow, requests are waiting on storage. Network bottlenecks are seen as saturated interfaces or many open connections that saturate bandwidth; ss shows sockets and the associated PIDs. A common misconception is to treat a single high load average as exclusively a C P U issue; load average counts processes waiting on C P U or uninterruptible input and output. For example, a database with heavy logging can raise load averages due to input and output waits even though C P U is moderate. The key takeaway is to map symptoms to the right resource before you act. Ask: which metric shows sustained abnormal values over time?

keyIdea.title: Map symptom to resource
keyIdea.text: High load can come from CPU or blocked I/O; confirm with targeted metrics (vmstat, iostat, top) before changing system settings.

content.html:
Core Concept Performance Bottlenecks

What a bottleneck is and why it matters

Understand the four resource classes and the specific metrics that indicate pressure on each. This prevents misdirected fixes and preserves system stability.

Resource Checklist
  • CPU: sustained high %user/%system, long run queue; use top/htop.
  • Memory: growing si/so in vmstat implies swapping and slowdown.
  • Disk I/O: high %util or avgqu-sz in iostat; long I/O wait times.
  • Network: high interface utilization or many sockets shown by ss.
Concrete analogy
Think of the system as a highway network: the CPU is a tollbooth lane, memory is parking for cars, disk is a ferry crossing with limited capacity, and network is the bridge bandwidth. Congestion at any one point slows all traffic.
Example metrics snippet
vmstat 1
procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st
 2  0  524288  102400  20480 5000000  0    100  0     1024  500 1000 30 10 50 10 0
The above shows swap-out activity (so) and non-zero run queue (r). This suggests combined memory pressure with runnable processes.
Key Takeaway

Always correlate multiple tools: a single metric can mislead. Use at least one tool for trends and one for process-level detail before acting.

screens.title: top vs htop — process-level monitoring
screens.subtitle: When to use top or htop and how to find a runaway process

narration.text: Both top and htop provide process-level visibility, but they present information differently and suit different workflows. top is universally available on RHEL and gives a compact, stable summary with C P U, memory, swap, and load averages. Use it when you need a minimal footprint or scripting-friendly output. htop is an enhanced, interactive alternative if installed: it offers color bars, easier sorting, scrolling through the process tree, and convenient keys to kill processes. In practice, you might start with htop to quickly identify a PID consuming many C P U cores and then use top or ps for scripted snapshots. A concrete example: after launching three C P U-bound yes loops, you will see three processes with near 100% per C P U in htop; identify their PIDs and assess which user owns them. A common misconception is that htop reveals more system facts than top; both read the same kernel data — htop only presents it more interactively. For safe corrective action, prefer sending a SIGTERM first and only escalate to SIGKILL with kill -9 if the process refuses to exit. When using these tools, note the system load averages as context; a high load with low C P U usage suggests blocked input and output instead. What process would you terminate first after confirming it is the cause?

keyIdea.title: Interactive vs universal
keyIdea.text: Use htop for quick interactive triage; use top for universal, low-overhead snapshots and scripting.

content.html:
Comparison top vs htop

Pick the right process viewer

Learn the strengths of each and a safe action pattern for misbehaving processes.

Interactive example (htop)
# Simulate CPU-bound tasks (run in separate terminal)
yes > /dev/null &
yes > /dev/null &
yes > /dev/null &
# Then run:
htop
# In htop you will see three 'yes' processes at top consuming CPU. Note their PIDs to act on them.
Tip: In htop press F6 to sort or F9 to send signals. Prefer SIGTERM before SIGKILL to let processes shut down gracefully.
Script-friendly snapshot (top)
top -b -n 1 | head -n 20
# Use this for logging a one-off snapshot for later analysis or for automation.
Common mistake: immediately rebooting a server instead of collecting a top or htop snapshot. Reboots can erase valuable live state that explains the root cause.
Key Takeaway

Use interactive tools to find candidates, then gather scripted snapshots and logs before terminating services.

screens.title: vmstat — reading swap and memory trends
screens.subtitle: Use vmstat to spot swapping and paging that indicate memory pressure

narration.text: vmstat reports virtual memory, processes, CPUs, and input and output activity in a compact table that is easy to sample over time. The most important columns for memory troubleshooting are si and so, swap in and swap out. When either column shows sustained non-zero values, the kernel is moving pages between R A M and swap space on disk; this is a strong sign of a memory bottleneck and will slow many workloads. Use vmstat 1 to observe trends at one-second intervals; short spikes are less alarming than continuous activity. Another useful indicator is the number of runnable processes in the 'r' column, which combined with 'si/so' helps you distinguish C P U-bound from memory-bound load. A concrete example: if vmstat shows high so and a large free memory decrease, you can consider adding R A M, reducing memory footprint, or tuning application caches. A common misconception is to swap away processes aggressively with swappiness tweaks without understanding workload patterns; that can hide underlying memory leaks. Always pair vmstat trends with process inspection (top/htop) and, if needed, use lsof to see which processes hold large files or open many file descriptors. End by asking: do you see persistent si/so over multiple samples or just occasional spikes?

keyIdea.title: si/so are memory alarms
keyIdea.text: Sustained vmstat si/so activity indicates a memory bottleneck; short spikes are less urgent but must be correlated with processes.

content.html:
Definition vmstat — si / so

Observe swap trends to find memory pressure

vmstat is best used for observing trends; combine short samples to decide if swapping is sustained or transient.

Example vmstat output
vmstat 1
procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st
 1  0  1048576  65536  10240 2000000  0    120   0    2048  300  800 25 10 40 25 0
 0  0  1153432  45000  10240 1950000  50   110  0    1024  250  650 35 12 30 23 0
Here you see so and si non-zero across samples: the system is actively swapping which indicates insufficient RAM for current workloads.
Practical steps
  • Confirm persistent si/so with vmstat 1 for several samples.
  • Use top/htop to find processes using most memory.
  • Consider adding RAM, tuning swappiness, or optimizing the culprit application.
Common Mistake

Tweaking swap settings before identifying the root cause can mask memory leaks and delay proper remediation.

screens.title: iostat — diagnosing disk I/O bottlenecks
screens.subtitle: Interpret %util, r/s, w/s and avgqu-sz to find storage contention

narration.text: iostat provides device-level metrics that help you decide if disks are the bottleneck. The key columns to watch are %util, r/s (reads per second), w/s (writes per second), and avgqu-sz (average queue size). %util approximates the percentage of time the device was busy; sustained values near 100% mean the device is saturated and further requests must wait. avgqu-sz shows how many requests are queued; growing queue sizes indicate that requests cannot be served quickly enough. For a concrete example, run iostat -x 1 during a heavy write workload and watch for a spike in %util and avgqu-sz on the target device (for example, sda). High input and output wait on C P U reports commonly accompany disk saturation and manifest as increased 'wa' time in top. A common misconception is to interpret any high read or write rate as a problem — throughput must be evaluated relative to %util and queue lengths. For remediation, consider examining application logging levels or database queries that cause many small writes, moving to faster storage, or reconfiguring input and output schedulers; always measure iostat again after changes to confirm improvement. What device shows the largest avgqu-sz in your next sample?

keyIdea.title: Queue lengths matter
keyIdea.text: High %util with growing avgqu-sz indicates storage saturation; address application patterns or storage speed, then re-measure.

content.html:
Definition iostat — disk metrics

Understand device utilization and queues

iostat is the right tool when you suspect storage is delaying I/O and slowing the whole system.

Sample iostat -x 1 output
Device:         r/s     w/s    rkB/s   wkB/s  avgrq-sz  avgqu-sz  await  r_await  w_await  svctm  %util
sda              0.5   100.0   16.0    800.0     8.16     12.34    120.0   120.0    120.0    1.00   98.5
Here %util is near 100% and avgqu-sz is non-trivial, indicating the device is busy and requests are queuing — a disk I/O bottleneck.
Investigation steps
  1. Run iostat -x 1 during peak activity to identify the device with highest %util and avgqu-sz.
  2. Correlate with application logs and consider whether logging or database writes are responsible.
  3. Test remediation: reduce logging, optimize queries, or move workload to faster storage, then re-run iostat.
Pro Tip

Small, frequent writes create high IOPS with poor throughput; consider batching or buffering in the application to reduce load on the device.

screens.title: Network connections and socket diagnostics with ss
screens.subtitle: Use ss to map active connections to processes and find network-related resource usage

narration.text: Network issues can create performance problems or mask other bottlenecks. ss replaces the older netstat and offers a quick way to list TCP and UDP sockets and the processes that own them. A typical first command is ss -tunap which shows TCP and UDP sockets, whether they are listening or established, and the PID/program name. Use this to detect unexpected listeners on ports or processes with many connections that could saturate bandwidth. For example, if a web process opens thousands of connections, you will see a high connection count with ss and can trace the PID to the service. A common mistake is to equate many connections with a network bottleneck immediately; you must also check interface throughput and round-trip times. Combine ss findings with ifstat or ip -s link and with application logs to assess whether traffic volumes or simply many idle sockets are the issue. If a socket is misbehaving, lsof -i can corroborate ss output by listing open files and sockets for the PID. Finally, document any changes you make to firewall rules or service configurations and verify the effect using ss again. Which process holds the most established sockets in your sample?

keyIdea.title: Map sockets to owners
keyIdea.text: ss -tunap helps you find which processes own network connections so you can target the right service when investigating network load.

content.html:
Process Flow ss & socket mapping

Find which process owns network connections

Use ss to identify heavy connection sources, then trace to PID and inspect the service.

Command example
ss -tunap
# Shows TCP/UDP sockets with PID and program name
# Look for many ESTAB lines or unexpected LISTEN sockets
If you find a suspicious PID, use lsof -p PID or lsof -i to inspect open sockets and file descriptors for that process.
Investigation checklist
  • Run ss -tunap and count established connections per PID.
  • Measure interface throughput with ip -s link or ifstat to confirm bandwidth pressure.
  • Correlate with service logs to see request patterns and whether connections are short-lived or persistent.
Why it matters

Identifying the owning process prevents you from blocking ports blindly and helps you tune service behavior or firewall rules appropriately.

screens.title: Systematic response to an unresponsive system
screens.subtitle: A stepwise troubleshooting routine to preserve evidence and restore service safely

narration.text: When a RHEL server becomes unresponsive, the first priority is to preserve diagnostic data while restoring service. Start by establishing scope: decide whether it is a single application or the whole host. Check load averages and swap activity to see if C P U or memory pressure is present, then confirm disk input and output and network status. Collect logs and kernel messages before making destructive changes; rebooting immediately often loses the most useful clues. If a process is responsible, attempt a graceful stop with a normal termination signal first. Use more forceful signals only when necessary and after capturing state. During each step, document what you observe and any commands you run so the chain of events is reproducible. A concrete example: if load averages are very high and swapping is visible, note the output of vmstat and top, capture a dmesg snapshot, and identify the PID consuming resources before killing it. A common misconception is to always use the forceful kill option; that can prevent graceful cleanup and make debugging harder. End by verifying the system recovers, then re-run monitoring to confirm the root cause is addressed. Which single fact would you record first in an incident log to help later analysis?

keyIdea.title: Preserve evidence, then act
keyIdea.text: Collect load, memory, disk and kernel messages before killing or rebooting. Document every step so root causes remain traceable.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › System Response Flow
Process
Systematic troubleshooting routine
Follow this routine to preserve data and identify the root cause
Core Skill
1
Scope & assess
Decide if problem is app-specific or system-wide and capture immediate metrics.
2
Capture evidence
Save output from top, vmstat, dmesg, and recent journal entries before altering state.
3
Isolate process
Identify PID(s) using high CPU, memory or I/O and note them for later analysis.
4
Recover safely
Try graceful stop signals, collect strace if needed, resort to force only when necessary.
5
Document & verify
Record what changed, re-monitor to confirm the fix, and schedule follow-up tuning.
Why this routine matters
  • Preserving logs and kernel messages helps you identify hardware faults or reproducible application failures.
  • Performing non-destructive checks first avoids losing transient evidence that a reboot or kill would remove.
  • Documenting commands and timestamps creates an incident timeline useful for postmortem and audits.
Concrete scenario
Example: high load and swapping
# capture before acting
uptime
vmstat 1 3
sudo dmesg -T | tail -n 50
ps -eo pid,ppid,cmd,%cpu,%mem --sort=-%cpu | head
Key Takeaway
Collect metrics and logs first. Recover service with minimal disturbance, then perform deeper analysis.
Common mistake
Rebooting immediately erases volatile data like process stacks and recent kernel messages.

screens.title: dmesg and journalctl — kernel and system logs
screens.subtitle: Using kernel messages and the system journal to find hardware and driver issues

narration.text: Kernel messages and the system journal are often the earliest indicators of low-level failures. The kernel ring buffer records hardware detection, driver errors, and critical events; the dmesg command reads that buffer. For example, if a disk controller or NIC driver is failing you will frequently see repeated errors in dmesg. The systemd journal, accessed via journalctl, aggregates service logs, kernel messages, and boot records with timestamps. A practical workflow is to snapshot dmesg output and then query journalctl for the time window around the incident. Use timestamps to correlate application errors with kernel events. A concrete example: after an input and output error, capture dmesg -T | tail -n 100, then run sudo journalctl -b -1 to review the previous boot for related messages. A common misconception is that dmesg and journalctl show identical data; they overlap but journalctl contains richer, persistent entries and structured metadata, whereas dmesg is the volatile kernel buffer. When investigating hardware or driver problems, always include both sources in your evidence. What kernel message would cause you to suspect hardware rather than a userland bug?

keyIdea.title: Kernel messages first
keyIdea.text: Use dmesg for low-level hardware and driver errors, and journalctl for persistent, timestamped service and system events.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Kernel & Journal
What to collect
Collect a dmesg snapshot and the relevant journal entries to find hardware errors or driver failures.
Commands
sudo dmesg -T | tail -n 100
sudo journalctl -b -1 --since "2024-11-01 09:50:00" --until "2024-11-01 10:05:00"
sudo journalctl -u myapp.service --since "10 minutes ago"
  • Use dmesg for direct kernel output with human timestamps (-T).
  • Use journalctl for service logs, historical boots, and full timestamps.
  • Correlate timestamps from both sources to form an incident timeline.
Example output and interpretation
[Fri Nov 1 10:00:01] ata1.00: exception Emask 0x0 SAct 0x0
[Fri Nov 1 10:00:01] ata1.00: failed command: READ FPDMA QUEUED
[Fri Nov 1 10:00:02] EXT4-fs error (device sda1): ext4_internal_error:...
Interpretation: repeated ATA or EXT4 errors point to disk hardware or driver problems rather than an application bug.
Key Takeaway
Always save dmesg and the relevant journal window before performing disruptive actions.

screens.title: strace — tracing system calls for application-level faults
screens.subtitle: How to attach, interpret, and use strace output to find file, permission, and syscall failures

narration.text: Strace traces the system calls a process makes and the signals it receives. It is invaluable when an application fails to open a file, hangs on input and output, or returns permission errors. There are two common modes: run a command under strace to trace startup, or attach to a running PID to observe live behavior. For example, to attach to PID 12345 you run sudo strace -p 12345; to trace a command you run strace -f -o trace. log mycommand. The -f option follows forks and -o writes output to a file for offline analysis. A concrete example: if your webapp cannot open its config, strace will show an open() call returning -13 (permission denied) and the exact path attempted. A common misconception is that strace solves performance problems directly; in fact it adds overhead and should be used briefly, with awareness that timing and behavior can change. When reading strace, look for failing return values, repeated retries, and long blocking syscalls like read()/write()/poll(). Always capture strace output before killing a process, and include the trace in your incident notes for later comparison. What failed system call would you search for first when an app reports "permission denied"?

keyIdea.title: See what the process asks the kernel
keyIdea.text: Use strace to reveal failing system calls and exact file paths; prefer short captures and log output for analysis.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › strace Deep Dive
Common commands
# Attach to running process
sudo strace -p 12345 -s 200 -o /tmp/strace-12345.log

# Trace a new command, following forks
sudo strace -f -o /tmp/trace.log mycommand arg1 arg2
Options shown: -s sets string size, -o writes output for later review, -f follows child processes. Use short captures to limit overhead.
Interpreting a snippet
open("/etc/myapp/config", O_RDONLY) = -1 EACCES (Permission denied)
poll([{fd=3, events=POLLIN}], 1, 60000) = 0 (Timeout)
write(1, "failed
", 7) = 7
Look for negative return values and errno labels (EACCES, ENOENT) to pinpoint the cause.
Example workflow
  1. Collect process id and small strace output to a file.
  2. Search the trace for failing calls like open, connect, stat, or read.
  3. Confirm filesystem paths and permissions or socket endpoints.
Caution
Strace can change timing and expose sensitive data. Use with care in production and rotate trace files promptly.
Key Takeaway
Strace shows exactly what syscalls fail and why. Use its failures to guide fixes for permissions, missing files, or socket errors.

screens.title: lsof — who holds a file or socket open?
screens.subtitle: Identify processes touching files, sockets, and deleted-but-held resources

narration.text: The lsof utility lists open files and the processes that hold them. In Linux, sockets, regular files, and even deleted files appear as open file descriptors. This is useful when you see "device busy" errors or need to find which process still writes to a log file that was rotated and deleted. Common commands include lsof -i to show network sockets with PIDs, lsof /path/to/file to see who is using a specific file, and lsof -p PID to inspect a process. For example, if a deleted log file continues to consume disk space, lsof | grep deleted will show the PID holding the inode open; terminating that process or restarting the service will release the space. Another misconception is that deleting a file always frees space; on Linux, the inode remains until all file descriptors are closed. Always confirm ownership and process intent before killing a service. As a closing question, when faced with a service holding a large deleted file open, would you restart the service or try to ask the process to close the file, and why? lsof — who holds a file or socket open? means use lsof to reveal which process holds file descriptors open, freeing space requires closing those descriptors or stopping the process.. In practical terms, identify processes touching files, sockets, and deleted-but-held resources. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Files can live after deletion
keyIdea.text: Use lsof to reveal which process holds file descriptors open, freeing space requires closing those descriptors or stopping the process.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › lsof Diagnostics
Essential lsof patterns
# list listening sockets and owning processes
sudo lsof -i -P -n

# find processes with deleted files
sudo lsof +L1

# who has /var/log/myapp.log open
sudo lsof /var/log/myapp.log
Flags: -P shows ports numerically, -n avoids DNS lookups, +L1 lists files with link count less than 1 (deleted).
Practical example
You rotated logs and removed the old file, but disk space didn't return. Run:
sudo lsof +L1 | grep /var/log
myapp   2345    root  log    8u   REG  8,1   10485760  /var/log/myapp.log (deleted)
Action: restart or gracefully ask process to close log; that releases space.
Pro Tip
Check owning PID and command line before killing. Prefer service restart if available to avoid lost state.

screens.title: Tuning cycle and safe remediation
screens.subtitle: Monitor, identify, change, and re-monitor — plus safe use of kill and reboot decisions

narration.text: Performance tuning is an iterative cycle: monitor to collect baseline metrics, identify the constrained resource, make a targeted change, and re-monitor to measure impact. Start with reliable metrics from tools like top, vmstat, iostat and ss. Once you identify the bottleneck, choose the least intrusive change first: tune application settings, reduce logging verbosity, or add caching. Only escalate to adding resources or replacing hardware when configuration changes are insufficient. Document every change and its timestamp so you can roll back if needed. When terminating processes, prefer graceful termination signals first: SIGTERM allows cleanup. SIGKILL (kill -9) forces immediate termination and should be a last resort because it prevents process cleanup and can leave resources in an inconsistent state. A typical tuning example: iostat -x shows high %util on a device; first reduce write amplification in the app or tune fsync behavior before increasing disk throughput or moving to faster storage. A common pitfall is making multiple unrelated changes at once; this makes measuring impact impossible. End by asking: what single metric will you re-check immediately after your change to verify improvement?

keyIdea.title: Iterate and measure
keyIdea.text: Make one targeted change at a time, document it, and re-measure to confirm the desired effect before proceeding.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Tuning Cycle
Tuning cycle
1. Monitor
Collect baseline metrics from top, vmstat, iostat, ss and logs.
2. Identify
Pinpoint the limited resource: CPU, memory, disk, or network.
3. Change
Make a minimal, reversible configuration change or restart a service if safe.
4. Re-monitor
Check the same metrics to confirm improvement and document results.
Example: high disk %util
  1. Observe iostat -x 1 and note %util and avgqu-sz spikes.
  2. Investigate application logging and query patterns that cause heavy writes.
  3. Reduce fsync frequency or rotate logs more often as a config change.
  4. Re-run iostat to confirm reduced %util before adding hardware.
Safe termination
Prefer sending SIGTERM (kill PID) to allow cleanup. Use SIGKILL (kill -9 PID) only when the process is unresponsive after graceful attempts, and after capturing strace or logs.
Avoid this
Don't reboot or use kill -9 before gathering logs; you may lose the evidence needed to find the root cause.
Key Takeaway
One small change at a time, measure impact, and document timestamps and outcomes for future tuning and audits.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Essential diagnostics and tools to keep in your toolkit

narration.text: Let's summarize the diagnostic tools and concepts you will return to when troubleshooting RHEL systems. dmesg surfaces kernel-level events and hardware driver errors, and should be captured early in an incident. strace exposes the system calls a process performs, showing precise failures like permission denied or missing files. lsof reveals which processes hold files or sockets open, which helps when disk space doesn't return after deleting files. Each of these tools complements monitoring utilities: dmesg and journalctl for persistent event context, strace for per-process syscall detail, and lsof for file descriptor ownership. When you combine these with real-time metrics you can construct a clear timeline and targeted remediation plan. Keep these three commands and their common flags in your day-to-day toolkit so you can capture evidence quickly and avoid destructive guesses. Which tool would you run first when you suspect a failing driver?

keyIdea.title: Diagnostic trio
keyIdea.text: dmesg, strace, and lsof each reveal different layers of system behavior — kernel, syscalls, and open resources.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Quick Reference
What to remember
Three compact concept cards to keep nearby during incidents
dmesg
Volatile kernel ring buffer; first place to check for hardware and driver errors.
strace
Traces system calls and signals. Use to find failing open/connect calls and errno values.
lsof
Lists open files and sockets. Perfect for finding deleted-but-held files or open network sockets.
Summary
Use these three tools together with monitoring output to build an accurate incident timeline and targeted fixes.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Performance metrics and diagnostic signs to watch for

narration.text: Finally, remember the core performance concepts that indicate where to focus your effort. A performance bottleneck is any resource—C P U, memory, disk input and output, or network—that limits overall system throughput. Load average measures processes waiting to run over 1, 5, and 15 minutes and helps indicate C P U contention. In vmstat, the si and so columns show swap activity; sustained swap in/out indicates memory pressure and is an important early warning. In iostat output, %util and avgqu-sz signal disk saturation and queueing; high values imply the disk is the bottleneck. Understanding which metric points to which resource will guide whether you tune an application, change configuration, or add resources. A short habit: when you start investigating, pick one primary metric to track before-and-after your change so you can prove improvement. Which metric will you pick for your next tuning task?

keyIdea.title: Metrics map to action
keyIdea.text: Map load, si/so, %util and avgqu-sz to CPU, memory, and disk actions to choose the correct remediation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Performance Signals
Metrics to trust
Three concise concept cards connecting metric to likely cause
Performance Bottleneck
A constrained resource (CPU, memory, disk, network) that limits overall system throughput and requires focused remediation.
Load Average
Average number of processes waiting to run. High sustained values suggest CPU contention or blocked I/O.
si / so (swap activity)
Swap-in and swap-out rates from vmstat. Persistent activity here points to memory pressure and potential performance degradation.
Takeaway
Monitor the right metric for the resource you believe is constrained, then make one change and re-measure to verify improvement.
